textbookText: 8.2.8 PHYLUM MOLLUSCA The term ‘mollusca’ was first applied by Aristotle to cuttle fish and is derived from latin word ‘mollis’ which means soft body. Phylum mollusca is the second largest phylum which comprises more than 100000 species. Among them 80000 species are gastropods.

General characters 1. They are mostly found in aquatic habitats, especially marine water, a few are freshwater forms and some are terrestrial. Most of the members of the phylum mollusca are free living and there are some parasitic forms (some gastropods).
2. Body is soft, unsegmented (except monoplacophora), and bilaterally symmetrical and
some are unsymmetrical.
3. Body is usually protected by exoskeleton in the form of calcareous shell. Skeleton may be internal or absent.
4. Their body can be divided into head, foot, mantle and visceral mass. 5. Head is distinct with mouth, eyes, tentacles, and other sensory organs except in

pelecypoda and scaphopoda. 6. Ventral surface consists of flat or plough like muscular foot which is variously modified for creeping, burrowing and swimming in water. 7. Mantle or pallium is a thick glandular fold of body wall on the dorsal surface. 8. Visceral mass consists of vital organs in compact form within the shell. 9. Alimentary canal is simple with anteriorly situated mouth and posterior anus. But in gastropods, scaphopods and cephalopods, intestine become U-shaped bringing the anus in anterior position. Radula or rasping organ in buccal cavity is usually present. 10. Circulatory system is open type (exception cephalopods) in which heart is with one or two auricles and one ventricle. Blood contains copper based respiratory pigment called haemocyanin. 11. Respiratory organs consist of numerous gills (branchiae) or ctenidium in aquatic forms, pulmonary sac or lungs in terrestrial forms. 12. Excretion occurs through a pair of metanephridia or kidneys. 13. Nervous system comprises paired ganglia (cerebral, pleural, pedal, visceral), connectives and nerves. 14. Sense organs are eyes, statocyst, osphradium (detect water chemistry) and tentacles. 15. They are usually dioecious and some are hermaphrodite too. 16. Fertilization is internal or external. Development is either direct or indirect with larva.

Unique features Soft bodied animals, calcareous exoskeleton in the form of shell or internal skeleton or absent, body divisible into head, mantle, visceral mass, ventral foot, open circulatory system, respiratory pigment haemocyanin, respiration through gills or ctenidia in aquatic and through lungs in terrestrial forms, osphradium as chemoreceptor

Classification Mollusca phylum is classified into six classes according to the symmetry, nature of foot, shell, mantle, gills, radula etc.

Class 1: Monoplacophora (Gr; monos-one; placo-plate) i. All marine forms. ii. Body is bilaterally symmetrical, internally segmented and with dome shaped mantle. iii. They have single limpet shaped flat shell and their foot is broad, flat and ventral. iv. Head is without eyes and tentacles. v. Sexes are separate.

Example: Neopilina Class 2: Amphineura (Gr; Amphi-both; neuron-nerve) i. They are all found in marine water. ii. Their body is dorso-ventrally flattened with shell and foot. Some of them are worm like without shell and foot. iii. Shell, if present, consist of 8 plates. iv. They have small head without eyes and tentacles. v. Radula, mantle and gills are present.

Example: Chiton, Neomenia Class 3: Scaphopoda (Gr; scapha-boat; podos-foot) i. They are exclusively marine forms. ii. Body is bilaterally symmetrical, enclosed within tusk-shaped shell opening at both ends. iii. Head is vestigial or not distinct, eyes and gills are absent. iv. Mouth is with filamentous tentacles and presence of radula. v. Foot is conical used for digging.

Example: Dentalium (Elephant tusk shell), Cadulus Class: 4 Gastropoda (Gr; gaster-belly; podos-foot) i. They are found in marine water, freshwater, land and also as parasitic form in echinoderms. ii. Body is unsegmented and asymmetrical. iii. Shell is present or absent or in reduced form. Shell is univalved and spirally coiled. iv. Head is distinct with eye tentacles and mouth. v. Muscular foot is broad and flat on ventral side. vi. Buccal cavity is with radula and anus is anteriorly situated. vii. Respiration by ctenidia (gills) or pulmonary sac or through general body surface.
Example: Pila (apple snail), Helix (garden snail), Limax (slug) etc.
Class 5: Pelecypoda or Bivalvia (Gr; pelekys-hatchet, podos-foot) i. Mostly marine, a few are freshwater forms.

ii. Body is bilaterally symmetrical, laterally compressed with bivalve shell. iii. Head is indistinct without tentacles, eyes, pharynx and radula. iv. Foot is hatchet or plough shaped. v. Some of them form pearl.
Example: Unio (freshwater mussel), Pecten, Pearl oyster etc.
